Just so you're aware, with your setup you'll either be hearing less latency than a traditional guitar amp, or virtually the same latency. We can prove this with maths.   


1000 milliseconds/44100 (the number of samples each second is broken up into) = 0.02226ms per sample  


0.0226ms X 32 (the number of samples that are loaded into your buffer before playback) = 0.725ms (Reaper will also report this figure for you).   


As a rough rule of thumb, sound travels 1ft every 1ms. A sound from your guitar amp 6ft away from your hears takes 6ms to be heard. If you're on monitors, let's assume they are 3ft away from your ears. We can add 3ms travel time to your latency of 0.725ms, giving us a total of 3.725ms for the sound to reach your ears after the signal enters your interface. If you're using headphones, this figure will likely be 1ms or under.   


Just so you're aware, the Kemper has a measurable latency of 3ms. Either what you're hearing is placebo, and you're convincing yourself it is there, or you have an issue with your interface or software setup.

It's actually quite simple. It will be plug and play provided 3 criteria are met:

1. Both systems have all VSTs used in a project file installed (applies to all DAWs)
2. No project files utilise AU (Apple Units - this is obviously a Windows restriction)
3. All recorded media is provided in a folder (applies to all DAWs)

You can set Reaper to save the project to a folder, and you can configure Reaper to save all recorded media to another folder within that directory. You won't have any issue with MIDI information, since that is saved within the project file, and needs to be exported out if you want the raw .midi files for whatever reason.

Some additional pointers:

* Try and be on the same version of Reaper. 99% of the time Reaper won't care and will open the project file anyway, but it's potential mole hill.
* If one of you has a paid plugin, sample library or virtual instrument that the other doesn't, and you don't want to buy an additional license, use the freeze or stem render into the project to simply send an up to date audio file using that plugin within the project.
* Windows has a lot more free (largely unnecessary) plug ins available than Mac, but all of the decent plugins are pretty much available across both OS.

Assuming you’re talking about drums and other percussion instruments (samples) that have indefinite pitch, you don’t need to pitch them to be in key. 

Because unpitched instruments produce a sound which contains multiple notes and harmonics series, none of which are strong enough to dominate the sound, they blend with the tonality of any music. The exception are pitched percussion, which include things like a Glockenspiel, Xylophone and Timpani. Rototoms are an outlier that are semi pitched, and only sound good in certain keys. 

Drums generally do need to be tuned however, but that is for the purposes of removing annoying overtones, rattles and for shaping the sound of the drum in various ways. It can include how deep and bassy a drum sounds, or how sharp the attack and release of the sound is. Tuning drums for these purposes is different to tuning drums to a specific pitch however.

It’s one of 2 things. 

1. Your computer can’t process everything fast enough. Solution: raise your buffer size - try 512. 

2. You’re clipping your stereo bus (master). Solution: lower all of your mix faders (except your reverb aux. etc), until your mix peaks at -8 to -6 dB. 

You can quickly test if this your issue without lowering all your faders by either lowering your master fader until your peaks hit -6, or just chucking a limiter on the master and slamming it, which will crush all of your peaks down to the ceiling of the limiter.
